\section[la liquidación]{la liquidación — the clearance sale; the settlement}

\label{lesson:ES-C631-liquidacion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the inflation, then the Spanish for the trade.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la liquidación}
\textbf{la liquidación} — \textquotedblleft{}the clearance sale; the settlement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La tienda cierra y hay liquidación.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The shop is closing and there is a clearance sale.}
\end{quote}

Also the final pay you receive when you leave a job.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{liquidación} is built on \emph{liquidar}, which comes from \emph{líquido}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{liquidus} 'fluid, clear' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la liquidación}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la liquidación}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la liquidación}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the inflation, then the Spanish for the trade, then say \emph{la liquidación} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la liquidación mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The clearance sale; the settlement\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[la rebaja]{la rebaja — the price cut; the sales}

\label{lesson:ES-C631-rebaja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the trade, then the Spanish for the clearance sale.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la rebaja}
\textbf{la rebaja} — \textquotedblleft{}the price cut; the sales\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En enero empiezan las rebajas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The sales start in January.}
\end{quote}

In Spain \emph{las rebajas} are the seasonal sales; Latin America often says \emph{las ofertas} or \emph{las liquidaciones}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rebaja} is built on \emph{rebajar} 'to lower', from \emph{bajo} 'low', which is inherited from Late Latin \emph{bassus} 'low' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la rebaja}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la rebaja}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la rebaja}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the trade, then the Spanish for the clearance sale, then say \emph{la rebaja} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la rebaja mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The price cut; the sales\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[la venta]{la venta — the sale}

\label{lesson:ES-C631-venta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the clearance sale, then the Spanish for the price cut.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la venta}
\textbf{la venta} — \textquotedblleft{}the sale\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La casa está en venta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The house is for sale.}
\end{quote}

\emph{En venta} — for sale.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{venta} is inherited from Latin \emph{vendita} 'sold', the participle of \emph{vendere} 'to sell' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la demanda]{la demanda — the demand; the lawsuit}

\label{lesson:ES-C631-demanda}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the price cut, then the Spanish for the sale.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la demanda}
\textbf{la demanda} — \textquotedblleft{}the demand; the lawsuit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay mucha demanda de pisos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is a lot of demand for flats.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La oferta y la demanda} — supply and demand. In law, a lawsuit.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{demanda} is built on \emph{demandar}, inherited from Latin \emph{demandare} 'to entrust', from \emph{mandare} 'to give into someone's hand, to order' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[valer]{valer — to be worth; to cost}

\label{lesson:ES-C631-valer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the sale, then the Spanish for the demand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: valer}
\textbf{valer} — \textquotedblleft{}to be worth; to cost\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
¿Cuánto vale este libro?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{How much is this book?}
\end{quote}

Irregular: \emph{valgo, valdré}. \emph{Vale} — OK, in Spain. \emph{No vale la pena} — it is not worth it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{valer} is inherited from Latin \emph{valere} 'to be strong, to be worth' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{valer}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{valer}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{valer}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the sale, then the Spanish for the demand, then say \emph{valer} again
\end{itemize}
